did_you_know.text: Here, the word shever does not mean something broken; it means grain or food for sale. This is a special use of the Hebrew root sh-b-r.
The phrase “go down to Egypt” fits a biblical expression that usually describes travel to Egypt as a descent. Egypt lies in the Nile Valley, while Canaan is generally more mountainous.
Benjamin and Joseph were Rachel’s sons, so Jacob was especially worried about Benjamin’s safety. Benjamin was the only son of Rachel still living at home with Jacob.
Here, “the children of Israel” refers to Jacob’s sons, since Jacob was also called Israel. Only later would Israel become the name of the entire nation.
Bowing facedown was a gesture of respect and submission before a ruler in the ancient Near East. It did not always mean worship; it could also be a formal sign of respect.
The brothers’ bowing recalls Joseph’s dreams, in which his brothers would bow to him. The story thus shows the dreams coming true, although the brothers do not yet realize it.
Many years had passed since Joseph was separated from his brothers, and he had become an Egyptian ruler. This creates dramatic irony: Joseph recognizes them, but they do not recognize him.
The phrase “the nakedness of the land” does not literally mean nudity; it refers to a country’s weak or exposed points. Joseph accuses them of searching for sensitive information about Egypt.
The brothers say that Joseph “is no more” without explicitly saying that he is dead. To them he has disappeared, but the reader already knows that he is alive and ruling Egypt.
Joseph keeps the brothers in custody for three days before offering a new arrangement. The short detention increases the tension and gives them time to confront their responsibility.
Here the brothers openly connect their present trouble with what they did to Joseph. They realize that ignoring their brother’s suffering had serious consequences.
The word melitz here means an interpreter or language mediator. Joseph spoke with his brothers through an interpreter, so they did not suspect that he understood them.
In biblical Hebrew, a malon is a travelers’ lodging place, such as a roadside station or inn. It does not necessarily mean a modern hotel with private rooms and services.
